### [Towhee · Locate the first actionable source-style violation](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/towhee)

Combine indentation and line-width diagnostics for a measured source file.

#### Locate the first actionable source-style violation

A line can have acceptable length but invalid indentation. Preserve both counts and show the earliest actionable row. The second line exceeds its width limit and the third makes an illegal indentation jump. The first problem is zero-based row 1.

[PEP 8, indentation and line length](https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/)

#### Run the framework with your own input

Install Blyx 0.2.1 and a Rust toolchain with a host linker, then run the versioned project. Each positional argument is a number or a comma-separated numerical vector. The CLI accepts up to 16 entries per vector. The imported module accepts longer inputs.

```
git clone --depth 1 --branch v0.1.0 https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-towhee.git
cd blyx-towhee
blyxc native-run project.blyx -- "0,4,12" "60,88,70" 4 80
```

[Project source](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-towhee/blob/v0.1.0/project.blyx) · [Native CLI downloads](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyxxxx/releases/tag/ecosystem-v0.1.0)

#### API and return values

Returns [clean, indentation violations, overlong rows, first problem row]. Supply aligned nonblank physical lines and their display widths. Invalid input returns an empty vector.

| Argument | Accepted input |
| --- | --- |
| indent | Vector of: nonnegative exact integer |
| widths | Vector of: nonnegative exact integer |
| step | positive exact integer |
| limit | positive exact integer |

#### Use the libraries independently

The framework vendors the same library source published in these two repositories. Each module has its own package page, input contract and regression suite.

[IndentSteps](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/indentsteps) · [LineWidth](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/linewidth) · [Framework installation](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/towhee)

#### Worked program

```blyx
// Towhee 0.1.0 · MIT OR Apache-2.0
// https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-towhee/tree/v0.1.0

fn indentsteps_max2(a: f64, b: f64) -> f64 {
    if a > b {
        return a;
    }
    b
}

fn indentsteps_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn indentsteps_counts(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= 0.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn indentsteps_compute(indent: vector, step: f64) -> vector {
    let mut errors = 0;
    let mut first = -1;
    let mut deepest = 0.0;
    let mut prev = 0.0;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(indent) {
        let col = at(indent, i);
        if (i == 0 && col != 0.0) || col % step != 0.0 || col > prev + step {
            if first < 0 {
                first = i;
            }
            errors += 1;
        }
        deepest = indentsteps_max2(deepest, col);
        prev = col;
        i += 1;
    }
    [errors, first, deepest]
}

// Audit fixed-step indentation measured on nonblank source lines.
// Returns [off-grid or illegal jump count, first offending row, deepest column]. The first nonblank row starts at zero and one line can increase by at most one indent step.
pub fn indentsteps_audit(indent: vector, step: f64) -> vector {
    if !indentsteps_counts(indent) { return []; }
    if !(step >= 1.0 && step <= 9007199254740991.0 && step % 1.0 == 0.0) { return []; }
    let result = indentsteps_compute(indent, step);
    if !indentsteps_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn linewidth_max2(a: f64, b: f64) -> f64 {
    if a > b {
        return a;
    }
    b
}

fn linewidth_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn linewidth_counts(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= 0.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn linewidth_compute(widths: vector, limit: f64) -> vector {
    let mut count = 0;
    let mut first = -1;
    let mut excess = 0.0;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(widths) {
        let gap = at(widths, i) - limit;
        if gap > 0.0 {
            if first < 0 {
                first = i;
            }
            count += 1;
            excess = linewidth_max2(excess, gap);
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    [count, first, excess]
}

// Find overlong source lines from measured display columns.
// Returns [overlong rows, first overlong row, largest excess]. The host selects a Unicode display-width convention and supplies widths including indentation.
pub fn linewidth_audit(widths: vector, limit: f64) -> vector {
    if !linewidth_counts(widths) { return []; }
    if !(limit >= 1.0 && limit <= 9007199254740991.0 && limit % 1.0 == 0.0) { return []; }
    let result = linewidth_compute(widths, limit);
    if !linewidth_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn towhee_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn towhee_counts(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= 0.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn towhee_compute(indent: vector, widths: vector, step: f64, limit: f64) -> vector {
    if len(indent) != len(widths) {
        return [];
    }
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(indent) {
        if at(indent, i) > at(widths, i) {
            return [];
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    let levels = indentsteps_audit(indent, step);
    let lines = linewidth_audit(widths, limit);
    if len(levels) == 0 || len(lines) == 0 {
        return [];
    }
    let mut first = at(levels, 1);
    if first < 0.0 || (at(lines, 1) >= 0.0 && at(lines, 1) < first) {
        first = at(lines, 1);
    }
    let mut clean = 0;
    if first < 0.0 {
        clean = 1;
    }
    [clean, at(levels, 0), at(lines, 0), first]
}

// Combine indentation and line-width diagnostics for a measured source file.
// Returns [clean, indentation violations, overlong rows, first problem row]. Supply aligned nonblank physical lines and their display widths.
pub fn towhee_lint(indent: vector, widths: vector, step: f64, limit: f64) -> vector {
    if !towhee_counts(indent) { return []; }
    if !towhee_counts(widths) { return []; }
    if !(step >= 1.0 && step <= 9007199254740991.0 && step % 1.0 == 0.0) { return []; }
    if !(limit >= 1.0 && limit <= 9007199254740991.0 && limit % 1.0 == 0.0) { return []; }
    let result = towhee_compute(indent, widths, step, limit);
    if !towhee_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn main() {
    let indent = [0, 4, 12];
    let widths = [60, 88, 70];
    let step = 4.0;
    let limit = 80.0;
    let result = towhee_lint(indent, widths, step, limit);
    if len(result) == 0 { println!("invalid"); return; }
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(result) {
        println!(at(result, i));
        i += 1;
    }
}
```

Expected output

```
0
1
1
1
```

#### Practice

Change indent = [0, 4], widths = [8, 12]. Predict the result, then run the program.

Hint

Returns [clean, indentation violations, overlong rows, first problem row]. Supply aligned nonblank physical lines and their display widths.

Solution

The result vector is [1, 0, 0, -1]. Compare its fields with the return layout in the API section.

Find

```blyx
    let indent = [0, 4, 12];
```

Replace with

```blyx
    let indent = [0, 4];
```

Find

```blyx
    let widths = [60, 88, 70];
```

Replace with

```blyx
    let widths = [8, 12];
```

Output after the change

```
1
0
0
-1
```

### [Bowerbird · Check a proposed dependency upgrade numerically](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/bowerbird)

Decide whether a proposed numeric-core dependency upgrade fits a declared version range.

#### Check a proposed dependency upgrade numerically

String sorting places 1.10 before 1.2. Check numeric ordering and the consumer's upper bound separately. Version 1.10.0 follows 1.2.9 and fits the interval below 2.0.0. The first changed component is minor.

[Semantic Versioning 2.0.0](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html)

#### Run the framework with your own input

Install Blyx 0.2.1 and a Rust toolchain with a host linker, then run the versioned project. Each positional argument is a number or a comma-separated numerical vector. The CLI accepts up to 16 entries per vector. The imported module accepts longer inputs.

```
git clone --depth 1 --branch v0.1.0 https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-bowerbird.git
cd blyx-bowerbird
blyxc native-run project.blyx -- "1,2,9" "1,10,0" "1,0,0" "2,0,0"
```

[Project source](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-bowerbird/blob/v0.1.0/project.blyx) · [Native CLI downloads](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyxxxx/releases/tag/ecosystem-v0.1.0)

#### API and return values

Returns [allowed upgrade, candidate versus installed, major/minor/patch index changed, within range]. Equal versions are allowed. This release handles numeric cores and explicit bounds. Invalid input returns an empty vector.

| Argument | Accepted input |
| --- | --- |
| installed | Vector of: nonnegative exact integer |
| candidate | Vector of: nonnegative exact integer |
| lower | Vector of: nonnegative exact integer |
| upper | Vector of: nonnegative exact integer |

#### Use the libraries independently

The framework vendors the same library source published in these two repositories. Each module has its own package page, input contract and regression suite.

[SemVerCore](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/semvercore) · [VersionBand](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/versionband) · [Framework installation](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/bowerbird)

#### Worked program

```blyx
// Bowerbird 0.1.0 · MIT OR Apache-2.0
// https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-bowerbird/tree/v0.1.0

fn semvercore_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn semvercore_counts(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= 0.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn semvercore_compute(left: vector, right: vector) -> vector {
    if len(left) != 3 || len(right) != 3 {
        return [];
    }
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < 3 {
        if at(left, i) < at(right, i) {
            return [-1, i];
        }
        if at(left, i) > at(right, i) {
            return [1, i];
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    [0, -1]
}

// Compare two numeric semantic-version cores lexicographically.
// Both inputs are [major, minor, patch]. Returns [ordering (-1,0,1), first differing component or -1]. Prerelease identifiers and build metadata are outside this core.
pub fn semvercore_compare(left: vector, right: vector) -> vector {
    if !semvercore_counts(left) { return []; }
    if !semvercore_counts(right) { return []; }
    let result = semvercore_compute(left, right);
    if !semvercore_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn versionband_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn versionband_counts(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= 0.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn versionband_compute(version: vector, lower: vector, upper: vector) -> vector {
    if len(version) != 3 || len(lower) != 3 || len(upper) != 3 {
        return [];
    }
    let mut bounds = 0;
    let mut lo = 0;
    let mut hi = 0;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < 3 {
        let v = at(version, i);
        let a = at(lower, i);
        let b = at(upper, i);
        if bounds == 0 {
            if a < b {
                bounds = -1;
            }
            if a > b {
                bounds = 1;
            }
        }
        if lo == 0 {
            if v < a {
                lo = -1;
            }
            if v > a {
                lo = 1;
            }
        }
        if hi == 0 {
            if v < b {
                hi = -1;
            }
            if v > b {
                hi = 1;
            }
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    if bounds != -1 {
        return [];
    }
    if lo < 0 {
        return [0, 1, 0];
    }
    if hi >= 0 {
        return [0, 0, 1];
    }
    [1, 0, 0]
}

// Check membership of a numeric-version core in a half-open dependency interval.
// Returns [inside, below lower, at or above upper]. All versions have three integer components and lower must precede upper.
pub fn versionband_contains(version: vector, lower: vector, upper: vector) -> vector {
    if !versionband_counts(version) { return []; }
    if !versionband_counts(lower) { return []; }
    if !versionband_counts(upper) { return []; }
    let result = versionband_compute(version, lower, upper);
    if !versionband_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn bowerbird_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn bowerbird_counts(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= 0.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn bowerbird_compute(installed: vector, candidate: vector, lower: vector, upper: vector) -> vector {
    let diff = semvercore_compare(candidate, installed);
    let allowed = versionband_contains(candidate, lower, upper);
    if len(diff) == 0 || len(allowed) == 0 {
        return [];
    }
    let mut ok = 0;
    if at(diff, 0) >= 0.0 && at(allowed, 0) == 1.0 {
        ok = 1;
    }
    [ok, at(diff, 0), at(diff, 1), at(allowed, 0)]
}

// Decide whether a proposed numeric-core dependency upgrade fits a declared version range.
// Returns [allowed upgrade, candidate versus installed, major/minor/patch index changed, within range]. Equal versions are allowed. This release handles numeric cores and explicit bounds.
pub fn bowerbird_upgrade(installed: vector, candidate: vector, lower: vector, upper: vector) -> vector {
    if !bowerbird_counts(installed) { return []; }
    if !bowerbird_counts(candidate) { return []; }
    if !bowerbird_counts(lower) { return []; }
    if !bowerbird_counts(upper) { return []; }
    let result = bowerbird_compute(installed, candidate, lower, upper);
    if !bowerbird_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn main() {
    let installed = [1, 2, 9];
    let candidate = [1, 10, 0];
    let lower = [1, 0, 0];
    let upper = [2, 0, 0];
    let result = bowerbird_upgrade(installed, candidate, lower, upper);
    if len(result) == 0 { println!("invalid"); return; }
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(result) {
        println!(at(result, i));
        i += 1;
    }
}
```

Expected output

```
1
1
1
1
```

#### Practice

Change candidate = [1, 1, 0]. Predict the result, then run the program.

Hint

Returns [allowed upgrade, candidate versus installed, major/minor/patch index changed, within range]. Equal versions are allowed. This release handles numeric cores and explicit bounds.

Solution

The result vector is [0, -1, 1, 1]. Compare its fields with the return layout in the API section.

Find

```blyx
    let candidate = [1, 10, 0];
```

Replace with

```blyx
    let candidate = [1, 1, 0];
```

```

-1
1
1
```

### [Albatross · Estimate a build's critical-path lower bound](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/albatross)

Estimate a build forest's scheduling lower bound from dependencies and worker capacity.

#### Estimate a build's critical-path lower bound

Adding workers cannot shorten a serial dependency chain. Compare total work with the longest dependency path before sizing a build pool. The four stages take eleven units of serial work. A dependency chain takes eight, so two workers cannot finish sooner than eight.

[Python, topological sorting](https://docs.python.org/3/library/graphlib.html)

#### Run the framework with your own input

Install Blyx 0.2.1 and a Rust toolchain with a host linker, then run the versioned project. Each positional argument is a number or a comma-separated numerical vector. The CLI accepts up to 16 entries per vector. The imported module accepts longer inputs.

```
git clone --depth 1 --branch v0.1.0 https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-albatross.git
cd blyx-albatross
blyxc native-run project.blyx -- "-1,0,0,2" "1,3,2,5" 2
```

[Project source](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-albatross/blob/v0.1.0/project.blyx) · [Native CLI downloads](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyxxxx/releases/tag/ecosystem-v0.1.0)

#### API and return values

Returns [critical path, total work, lower bound with given workers, deepest stage count]. The capacity bound assumes divisible worker time; actual nonpreemptive schedules can take longer. Invalid input returns an empty vector.

| Argument | Accepted input |
| --- | --- |
| parents | Vector of: exact signed integer |
| durations | Vector of: nonnegative finite number |
| workers | positive exact integer |

#### Use the libraries independently

The framework vendors the same library source published in these two repositories. Each module has its own package page, input contract and regression suite.

[DagOrder](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/dagorder) · [RunDuration](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/runduration) · [Framework installation](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/albatross)

#### Per-worker model-state memory

Specify the number of parameters, worker count, zero-based rank, ZeRO stage, and bytes per parameter for weights, gradients and optimizer state. Stage 1 partitions optimizer state, stage 2 also partitions gradients, and stage 3 also partitions weights. Remainders go to the lowest ranks. The minimum-rank search budgets the largest rank. Results are signed 64-bit byte counts under balanced partitioning. The reserve is supplied by the caller. Measure activations, communication buffers, fragmentation and runtime overhead for your own model. A fit in this arithmetic model does not establish throughput or a successful distributed training run.

```
albatross state 2199023255552 512 0 3 2 2 12
albatross min-ranks 2199023255552 3 2 2 12 85899345920 17179869184 4096
```

[Albatross native downloads](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-albatross/releases/tag/v0.2.0) · [Input formats, compiler revision and API example](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-albatross/blob/v0.2.0/SCALE.md) · [Read the experiment and download measurements](https://www.blyx-lang.space/articles/training-in-factors)

#### Worked program

```blyx
// Albatross 0.1.0 · MIT OR Apache-2.0
// https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-albatross/tree/v0.1.0

fn dagorder_num(value: i64) -> f64 {
    at([value], 0)
}

fn dagorder_slot(key: f64, size: i64) -> i64 {
    let mut lo = 0;
    let mut hi = size;
    while lo < hi {
        let mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if at([mid], 0) < key {
            lo = mid + 1;
        } else {
            hi = mid;
        }
    }
    lo
}

fn dagorder_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn dagorder_integers(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= -9007199254740991.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn dagorder_compute(parents: vector) -> vector {
    let mut roots = 0;
    let mut deepest = 0;
    let mut leaf = -1;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(parents) {
        let parent = at(parents, i);
        if parent < -1.0 || parent >= dagorder_num(i) {
            return [];
        }
        if parent == -1.0 {
            roots += 1;
        }
        let mut steps = 1;
        let mut next = parent;
        while next >= 0.0 {
            let idx = dagorder_slot(next, i);
            next = at(parents, idx);
            steps += 1;
        }
        if steps > deepest {
            deepest = steps;
            leaf = i;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    [roots, deepest, leaf]
}

// Validate indexed dependencies in an ordered build forest.
// Each stage names one earlier parent or -1 for a root. Returns [root count, maximum chain length in stages, first stage with that depth]. Empty forests have zero depth.
pub fn dagorder_forest(parents: vector) -> vector {
    if !dagorder_integers(parents) { return []; }
    let result = dagorder_compute(parents);
    if !dagorder_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn runduration_max2(a: f64, b: f64) -> f64 {
    if a > b {
        return a;
    }
    b
}

fn runduration_num(value: i64) -> f64 {
    at([value], 0)
}

fn runduration_slot(key: f64, size: i64) -> i64 {
    let mut lo = 0;
    let mut hi = size;
    while lo < hi {
        let mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if at([mid], 0) < key {
            lo = mid + 1;
        } else {
            hi = mid;
        }
    }
    lo
}

fn runduration_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn runduration_integers(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= -9007199254740991.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn runduration_magnitudes(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= 0.0 && value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn runduration_compute(parents: vector, durations: vector) -> vector {
    if len(parents) != len(durations) {
        return [];
    }
    let mut best = -1.0;
    let mut leaf = -1;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(parents) {
        let nextparent = at(parents, i);
        if nextparent < -1.0 || nextparent >= runduration_num(i) {
            return [];
        }
        let mut cost = at(durations, i);
        let mut next = nextparent;
        while next >= 0.0 {
            let idx = runduration_slot(next, i);
            cost += at(durations, idx);
            next = at(parents, idx);
        }
        if cost > best {
            best = cost;
            leaf = i;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    [runduration_max2(best, 0.0), leaf, sum(durations)]
}

// Find the critical-path time in a forest of dependent tasks.
// Returns [longest path duration, first endpoint at that duration, total sequential work]. Each input row depends on one previous row or -1. Durations share a unit.
pub fn runduration_path(parents: vector, durations: vector) -> vector {
    if !runduration_integers(parents) { return []; }
    if !runduration_magnitudes(durations) { return []; }
    let result = runduration_compute(parents, durations);
    if !runduration_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn albatross_max2(a: f64, b: f64) -> f64 {
    if a > b {
        return a;
    }
    b
}

fn albatross_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn albatross_integers(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= -9007199254740991.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn albatross_magnitudes(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= 0.0 && value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn albatross_compute(parents: vector, durations: vector, workers: f64) -> vector {
    let shape = dagorder_forest(parents);
    let timing = runduration_path(parents, durations);
    if len(shape) == 0 || len(timing) == 0 {
        return [];
    }
    [at(timing, 0), at(timing, 2), albatross_max2(at(timing, 0), at(timing, 2) / workers), at(shape, 1)]
}

// Estimate a build forest's scheduling lower bound from dependencies and worker capacity.
// Returns [critical path, total work, lower bound with given workers, deepest stage count]. The capacity bound assumes divisible worker time; actual nonpreemptive schedules can take longer.
pub fn albatross_schedule(parents: vector, durations: vector, workers: f64) -> vector {
    if !albatross_integers(parents) { return []; }
    if !albatross_magnitudes(durations) { return []; }
    if !(workers >= 1.0 && workers <= 9007199254740991.0 && workers % 1.0 == 0.0) { return []; }
    let result = albatross_compute(parents, durations, workers);
    if !albatross_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn main() {
    let parents = [-1, 0, 0, 2];
    let durations = [1, 3, 2, 5];
    let workers = 2.0;
    let result = albatross_schedule(parents, durations, workers);
    if len(result) == 0 { println!("invalid"); return; }
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(result) {
        println!(at(result, i));
        i += 1;
    }
}
```

Expected output

```
11
8
3
```

### [Chaffinch · Reconcile two sorted snapshots with repeated keys](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/chaffinch)

Reconcile sorted collection snapshots without materializing their union.

#### Reconcile two sorted snapshots with repeated keys

A duplicate row should not look like a newly added key. Compare distinct sets and report repeated occurrences separately. The new snapshot adds key 3, removes key 1 and retains 2 and 4. The repeated 2 contributes one duplicate occurrence.

[Python, grouping consecutive keys](https://docs.python.org/3/library/itertools.html#itertools.groupby)

#### Run the framework with your own input

Install Blyx 0.2.1 and a Rust toolchain with a host linker, then run the versioned project. Each positional argument is a number or a comma-separated numerical vector. The CLI accepts up to 16 entries per vector. The imported module accepts longer inputs.

```
git clone --depth 1 --branch v0.1.0 https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-chaffinch.git
cd blyx-chaffinch
blyxc native-run project.blyx -- "1,1,2,4" "2,2,3,4"
```

[Project source](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-chaffinch/blob/v0.1.0/project.blyx) · [Native CLI downloads](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyxxxx/releases/tag/ecosystem-v0.1.0)

#### API and return values

Returns [added unique keys, removed unique keys, retained keys, duplicate occurrences in the new snapshot]. Inputs are sorted, allowing forward-only scans. Invalid input returns an empty vector.

| Argument | Accepted input |
| --- | --- |
| old | Vector of: exact signed integer |
| fresh | Vector of: exact signed integer |

#### Use the libraries independently

The framework vendors the same library source published in these two repositories. Each module has its own package page, input contract and regression suite.

[SortRuns](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/sortruns) · [MergeCounts](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/mergecounts) · [Framework installation](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/chaffinch)

#### Reduce sparse worker gradients

Each worker writes numeric pairs, one coordinate and one summed gradient per CSV row, in ascending coordinate order. Duplicates are allowed. Merge two runs in linear time, compensate for floating-point cancellation, then divide by the number of training examples across the two workers. Missing coordinates contribute zero. The denominator is the global example count, including examples with a zero gradient. The CLI accepts finite gradients and exact integer coordinates from 0 to 9,007,199,254,740,991. Input and output are in memory. A merge processes two worker files and does not provide a network collective.

```
chaffinch reduce 4 fixtures/worker-a.csv fixtures/worker-b.csv
```

[Chaffinch native downloads](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-chaffinch/releases/tag/v0.2.0) · [Input formats, compiler revision and API example](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-chaffinch/blob/v0.2.0/SCALE.md) · [Read the experiment and download measurements](https://www.blyx-lang.space/articles/training-in-factors)

#### Worked program

```blyx
// Chaffinch 0.1.0 · MIT OR Apache-2.0
// https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-chaffinch/tree/v0.1.0

fn sortruns_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn sortruns_integers(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= -9007199254740991.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn sortruns_compute(values: vector) -> vector {
    if len(values) == 0 {
        return [0, 0, 0];
    }
    let mut kinds = 0;
    let mut run = 0;
    let mut best = 0;
    let mut key = at(values, 0);
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let current = at(values, i);
        if i > 0 && current < at(values, i - 1) {
            return [];
        }
        if i == 0 || current != at(values, i - 1) {
            kinds += 1;
            run = 0;
        }
        run += 1;
        if run > best {
            best = run;
            key = current;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    [kinds, best, key]
}

// Summarize equal-value runs in a nondecreasing integer stream.
// Returns [distinct values, longest run length, first key with that run]. Empty input returns [0,0,0]. Rejects descending keys.
pub fn sortruns_profile(values: vector) -> vector {
    if !sortruns_integers(values) { return []; }
    let result = sortruns_compute(values);
    if !sortruns_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn mergecounts_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn mergecounts_integers(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= -9007199254740991.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn mergecounts_compute(left: vector, right: vector) -> vector {
    let mut k = 1;
    while k < len(left) {
        if at(left, k) < at(left, k - 1) {
            return [];
        }
        k += 1;
    }
    k = 1;
    while k < len(right) {
        if at(right, k) < at(right, k - 1) {
            return [];
        }
        k += 1;
    }
    let mut a = 0;
    let mut b = 0;
    let mut shared = 0;
    let mut only_a = 0;
    let mut only_b = 0;
    while a < len(left) || b < len(right) {
        let mut key = 0.0;
        if b == len(right) || (a < len(left) && at(left, a) < at(right, b)) {
            key = at(left, a);
            only_a += 1;
        } else {
            if a == len(left) || at(right, b) < at(left, a) {
                key = at(right, b);
                only_b += 1;
            } else {
                key = at(left, a);
                shared += 1;
            }
        }
        while a < len(left) && at(left, a) == key {
            a += 1;
        }
        while b < len(right) && at(right, b) == key {
            b += 1;
        }
    }
    [shared, only_a, only_b]
}

// Count unique keys shared or exclusive to two sorted streams.
// Returns [shared, left-only, right-only]. Repeats within a stream count once. Both streams must be nondecreasing; the merge uses two forward cursors.
pub fn mergecounts_sets(left: vector, right: vector) -> vector {
    if !mergecounts_integers(left) { return []; }
    if !mergecounts_integers(right) { return []; }
    let result = mergecounts_compute(left, right);
    if !mergecounts_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn chaffinch_num(value: i64) -> f64 {
    at([value], 0)
}

fn chaffinch_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn chaffinch_integers(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= -9007199254740991.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn chaffinch_compute(old: vector, fresh: vector) -> vector {
    let previous = sortruns_profile(old);
    let current = sortruns_profile(fresh);
    let merged = mergecounts_sets(old, fresh);
    if len(previous) == 0 || len(current) == 0 || len(merged) == 0 {
        return [];
    }
    [at(merged, 2), at(merged, 1), at(merged, 0), chaffinch_num(len(fresh)) - at(current, 0)]
}

// Reconcile sorted collection snapshots without materializing their union.
// Returns [added unique keys, removed unique keys, retained keys, duplicate occurrences in the new snapshot]. Inputs are sorted, allowing forward-only scans.
pub fn chaffinch_reconcile(old: vector, fresh: vector) -> vector {
    if !chaffinch_integers(old) { return []; }
    if !chaffinch_integers(fresh) { return []; }
    let result = chaffinch_compute(old, fresh);
    if !chaffinch_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn main() {
    let old = [1, 1, 2, 4];
    let fresh = [2, 2, 3, 4];
    let result = chaffinch_reconcile(old, fresh);
    if len(result) == 0 { println!("invalid"); return; }
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(result) {
        println!(at(result, i));
        i += 1;
    }
}
```

Expected output

```
1
1
2
1
```

#### Practice

Change old = [], fresh = [9, 9]. Predict the result, then run the program.

Hint

Returns [added unique keys, removed unique keys, retained keys, duplicate occurrences in the new snapshot]. Inputs are sorted, allowing forward-only scans.

Solution

The result vector is [1, 0, 0, 1]. Compare its fields with the return layout in the API section.

Find

```blyx
    let old = [1, 1, 2, 4];
```

Replace with

```blyx
    let old = [];
```

Find

```blyx
    let fresh = [2, 2, 3, 4];
```

Replace with

```blyx
    let fresh = [9, 9];
```

Output after the change

```
1
0
0
1
```

### [Pelican · Compare merged reads with aligned per-request reads](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/pelican)

Compare per-request aligned I/O with coalesced unaligned reads for a sorted trace.

#### Compare merged reads with aligned per-request reads

Merging requests saves seeks but can read unused gap bytes. Report each cost explicitly before changing a storage access pattern. The example's two merged ranges fetch ten bytes including a one-byte gap. Independent eight-byte-aligned reads would fetch 24.

[POSIX, pread and pwrite offsets](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pread.html)

#### Run the framework with your own input

Install Blyx 0.2.1 and a Rust toolchain with a host linker, then run the versioned project. Each positional argument is a number or a comma-separated numerical vector. The CLI accepts up to 16 entries per vector. The imported module accepts longer inputs.

```
git clone --depth 1 --branch v0.1.0 https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-pelican.git
cd blyx-pelican
blyxc native-run project.blyx -- "0,5,20" "4,3,2" 1 8
```

[Project source](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-pelican/blob/v0.1.0/project.blyx) · [Native CLI downloads](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyxxxx/releases/tag/ecosystem-v0.1.0)

#### API and return values

Returns [independent aligned bytes, coalesced read count, coalesced bytes, bridge-gap bytes]. Values describe two explicitly defined read strategies. Invalid input returns an empty vector.

| Argument | Accepted input |
| --- | --- |
| starts | Vector of: nonnegative exact integer |
| lengths | Vector of: positive exact integer |
| gap | nonnegative exact integer |
| block | positive exact integer |

#### Use the libraries independently

The framework vendors the same library source published in these two repositories. Each module has its own package page, input contract and regression suite.

[BlockSpan](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/blockspan) · [CoalesceIO](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/coalesceio) · [Framework installation](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/pelican)

#### Worked program

```blyx
// Pelican 0.1.0 · MIT OR Apache-2.0
// https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-pelican/tree/v0.1.0

fn blockspan_ceilpos(value: f64) -> f64 {
    let rest = value % 1.0;
    if rest > 0.0 {
        return value - rest + 1.0;
    }
    value
}

fn blockspan_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn blockspan_compute(offset: f64, length: f64, block: f64) -> vector {
    if length == 0.0 {
        return [offset, 0, 0];
    }
    let stop = offset + length;
    if stop > 9007199254740991.0 {
        return [];
    }
    let first = offset - offset % block;
    let tail = blockspan_ceilpos(stop / block) * block;
    if tail > 9007199254740991.0 {
        return [];
    }
    [first, tail - first, offset - first]
}

// Expand a byte request to whole storage blocks.
// Returns [aligned start, bytes to read, requested start within read]. A zero-length request incurs zero reads. Counts must remain exactly representable.
pub fn blockspan_align(offset: f64, length: f64, block: f64) -> vector {
    if !(offset >= 0.0 && offset <= 9007199254740991.0 && offset % 1.0 == 0.0) { return []; }
    if !(length >= 0.0 && length <= 9007199254740991.0 && length % 1.0 == 0.0) { return []; }
    if !(block >= 1.0 && block <= 9007199254740991.0 && block % 1.0 == 0.0) { return []; }
    let result = blockspan_compute(offset, length, block);
    if !blockspan_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn coalesceio_max2(a: f64, b: f64) -> f64 {
    if a > b {
        return a;
    }
    b
}

fn coalesceio_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn coalesceio_positive_counts(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= 1.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn coalesceio_counts(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= 0.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn coalesceio_compute(starts: vector, lengths: vector, gap: f64) -> vector {
    if len(starts) != len(lengths) {
        return [];
    }
    let mut end = 0.0;
    let mut fetched = 0.0;
    let mut extra = 0.0;
    let mut reads = 0;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(starts) {
        let a = at(starts, i);
        let b = a + at(lengths, i);
        if b > 9007199254740991.0 || (i > 0 && a < at(starts, i - 1)) {
            return [];
        }
        if i == 0 || a - end > gap {
            reads += 1;
            fetched += b - a;
            end = b;
        } else {
            extra += coalesceio_max2(0.0, a - end);
            fetched += coalesceio_max2(0.0, b - end);
            end = coalesceio_max2(end, b);
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    [reads, fetched, extra]
}

// Count merged reads and extra gap bytes for sorted byte requests.
// Returns [merged reads, fetched bytes, extra bytes spanning gaps]. Overlapping bytes are counted once. Positive request lengths are required.
pub fn coalesceio_plan(starts: vector, lengths: vector, gap: f64) -> vector {
    if !coalesceio_counts(starts) { return []; }
    if !coalesceio_positive_counts(lengths) { return []; }
    if !(gap >= 0.0 && gap <= 9007199254740991.0 && gap % 1.0 == 0.0) { return []; }
    let result = coalesceio_compute(starts, lengths, gap);
    if !coalesceio_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn pelican_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn pelican_positive_counts(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= 1.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn pelican_counts(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= 0.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn pelican_compute(starts: vector, lengths: vector, gap: f64, block: f64) -> vector {
    let merged = coalesceio_plan(starts, lengths, gap);
    if len(merged) == 0 {
        return [];
    }
    let mut total = 0.0;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(starts) {
        let span = blockspan_align(at(starts, i), at(lengths, i), block);
        if len(span) == 0 {
            return [];
        }
        total += at(span, 1);
        if total > 9007199254740991.0 {
            return [];
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    [total, at(merged, 0), at(merged, 1), at(merged, 2)]
}

// Compare per-request aligned I/O with coalesced unaligned reads for a sorted trace.
// Returns [independent aligned bytes, coalesced read count, coalesced bytes, bridge-gap bytes]. Values describe two explicitly defined read strategies.
pub fn pelican_reads(starts: vector, lengths: vector, gap: f64, block: f64) -> vector {
    if !pelican_counts(starts) { return []; }
    if !pelican_positive_counts(lengths) { return []; }
    if !(gap >= 0.0 && gap <= 9007199254740991.0 && gap % 1.0 == 0.0) { return []; }
    if !(block >= 1.0 && block <= 9007199254740991.0 && block % 1.0 == 0.0) { return []; }
    let result = pelican_compute(starts, lengths, gap, block);
    if !pelican_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn main() {
    let starts = [0, 5, 20];
    let lengths = [4, 3, 2];
    let gap = 1.0;
    let block = 8.0;
    let result = pelican_reads(starts, lengths, gap, block);
    if len(result) == 0 { println!("invalid"); return; }
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(result) {
        println!(at(result, i));
        i += 1;
    }
}
```

### [Nightingale · Bound a percentile from histogram counts](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/nightingale)

Bound a percentile from histogram counts without inventing a within-bin value.

#### Bound a percentile from histogram counts

Histogram counts identify the bucket containing a percentile, not its exact location. Return the interval before deciding whether a threshold was breached. The median is the fourth observation and lies in the 10–30 bucket. A threshold of 20 lies inside that bucket, so the classification stays unresolved.

[Prometheus, histogram quantiles](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/histograms/)

#### Run the framework with your own input

Install Blyx 0.2.1 and a Rust toolchain with a host linker, then run the versioned project. Each positional argument is a number or a comma-separated numerical vector. The CLI accepts up to 16 entries per vector. The imported module accepts longer inputs.

```
git clone --depth 1 --branch v0.1.0 https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-nightingale.git
cd blyx-nightingale
blyxc native-run project.blyx -- "2,6" "0,10,30" 0.5 20
```

[Project source](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-nightingale/blob/v0.1.0/project.blyx) · [Native CLI downloads](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyxxxx/releases/tag/ecosystem-v0.1.0)

#### API and return values

Returns [lower bound, upper bound, rank, classification]. Classification is -1 when the whole interval is below threshold, 1 when entirely at or above, and 0 when the bins cannot decide. The upper-bound comparison is deliberately conservative. Invalid input returns an empty vector.

| Argument | Accepted input |
| --- | --- |
| counts | Vector of: nonnegative exact integer |
| edges | Vector of: finite number |
| probability | probability in [0,1] |
| threshold | finite number |

#### Use the libraries independently

The framework vendors the same library source published in these two repositories. Each module has its own package page, input contract and regression suite.

[HistQuantile](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/histquantile) · [RankBand](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/rankband) · [Framework installation](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages/nightingale)

#### Worked program

```blyx
// Nightingale 0.1.0 · MIT OR Apache-2.0
// https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-nightingale/tree/v0.1.0

fn histquantile_max2(a: f64, b: f64) -> f64 {
    if a > b {
        return a;
    }
    b
}

fn histquantile_ceilpos(value: f64) -> f64 {
    let rest = value % 1.0;
    if rest > 0.0 {
        return value - rest + 1.0;
    }
    value
}

fn histquantile_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn histquantile_counts(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= 0.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn histquantile_compute(counts: vector, probability: f64) -> vector {
    let total = sum(counts);
    if total <= 0.0 || total > 9007199254740991.0 {
        return [];
    }
    let rank = histquantile_max2(1.0, histquantile_ceilpos(total * probability));
    let mut seen = 0.0;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(counts) {
        seen += at(counts, i);
        if seen >= rank {
            return [i, rank, total];
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    []
}

// Locate a nearest-rank quantile in noncumulative histogram counts.
// Returns [bucket index, one-based rank, total observations]. At probability zero select the first occupied bucket. Empty histograms are invalid.
pub fn histquantile_bucket(counts: vector, probability: f64) -> vector {
    if !histquantile_counts(counts) { return []; }
    if !(probability >= 0.0 && probability <= 1.0) { return []; }
    let result = histquantile_compute(counts, probability);
    if !histquantile_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn rankband_num(value: i64) -> f64 {
    at([value], 0)
}

fn rankband_slot(key: f64, size: i64) -> i64 {
    let mut lo = 0;
    let mut hi = size;
    while lo < hi {
        let mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if at([mid], 0) < key {
            lo = mid + 1;
        } else {
            hi = mid;
        }
    }
    lo
}

fn rankband_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn rankband_compute(edges: vector, index: f64) -> vector {
    if len(edges) < 2 || index >= rankband_num(len(edges) - 1) {
        return [];
    }
    let mut i = 1;
    while i < len(edges) {
        if at(edges, i) <= at(edges, i - 1) {
            return [];
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    let j = rankband_slot(index, len(edges));
    let a = at(edges, j);
    let b = at(edges, j + 1);
    [a, b, b - a]
}

// Look up the finite interval represented by a histogram bin.
// Edges must be strictly increasing. Returns [lower edge, upper edge, span]. Bins are half-open except the last, which may include its upper edge.
pub fn rankband_interval(edges: vector, index: f64) -> vector {
    if !rankband_finite(edges) { return []; }
    if !(index >= 0.0 && index <= 9007199254740991.0 && index % 1.0 == 0.0) { return []; }
    let result = rankband_compute(edges, index);
    if !rankband_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn nightingale_finite(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value - value == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn nightingale_counts(values: vector) -> bool {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(values) {
        let value = at(values, i);
        if !(value >= 0.0 && value <= 9007199254740991.0 && value % 1.0 == 0.0) {
            return false;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

fn nightingale_compute(counts: vector, edges: vector, probability: f64, threshold: f64) -> vector {
    if len(edges) != len(counts) + 1 {
        return [];
    }
    let rank = histquantile_bucket(counts, probability);
    if len(rank) == 0 {
        return [];
    }
    let band = rankband_interval(edges, at(rank, 0));
    if len(band) == 0 {
        return [];
    }
    let mut decision = 0;
    if at(band, 1) < threshold {
        decision = -1;
    }
    if at(band, 0) >= threshold {
        decision = 1;
    }
    [at(band, 0), at(band, 1), at(rank, 1), decision]
}

// Bound a percentile from histogram counts without inventing a within-bin value.
// Returns [lower bound, upper bound, rank, classification]. Classification is -1 when the whole interval is below threshold, 1 when entirely at or above, and 0 when the bins cannot decide. The upper-bound comparison is deliberately conservative.
pub fn nightingale_quantile(counts: vector, edges: vector, probability: f64, threshold: f64) -> vector {
    if !nightingale_counts(counts) { return []; }
    if !nightingale_finite(edges) { return []; }
    if !(probability >= 0.0 && probability <= 1.0) { return []; }
    if !(threshold - threshold == 0.0) { return []; }
    let result = nightingale_compute(counts, edges, probability, threshold);
    if !nightingale_finite(result) { return []; }
    result
}

fn main() {
    let counts = [2, 6];
    let edges = [0, 10, 30];
    let probability = 0.5;
    let threshold = 20.0;
    let result = nightingale_quantile(counts, edges, probability, threshold);
    if len(result) == 0 { println!("invalid"); return; }
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(result) {
        println!(at(result, i));
        i += 1;
    }
}
```

Expected output

```
10
30
4
0
```

#### Practice

Change probability = 0.25. Predict the result, then run the program.

Hint

Returns [lower bound, upper bound, rank, classification]. Classification is -1 when the whole interval is below threshold, 1 when entirely at or above, and 0 when the bins cannot decide. The upper-bound comparison is deliberately conservative.

Solution

The result vector is [0, 10, 2, -1]. Compare its fields with the return layout in the API section.

Find

```blyx
    let probability = 0.5;
```

Replace with

```blyx
    let probability = 0.25;
```

Output after the change

```
0
10
2
-1
```

## Local toolchain

### [Install and verify Blyx](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/installation)

Choose a binary or package manager, locate the executable, and verify the exact compiler version.

#### Choose how to run the course

Every tutorial with an editor can run in the browser. A local installation lets you save source files and invoke the command-line tool blyxc. Building a native executable also requires rustc and a host linker on the machine doing the build.

#### Download a release archive

Choose the Windows x86-64 ZIP, Linux x86-64 tarball, or Apple Silicon macOS tarball from the download page. Compare its SHA-256 digest with the entry for the same filename in SHA256SUMS. Extract the archive and add the directory containing blyxc to PATH. In PowerShell you can run .\blyxc.exe directly from the extracted directory.

#### Install with Homebrew

On Apple Silicon macOS or x86-64 Linux, the project tap installs the published compiler binary and checks the archive checksum.

```
brew install rahulchaube1/blyx/blyx
```

#### Install on Windows with Scoop

On Windows x64, add the project bucket once from PowerShell, then install the compiler and check its version. Scoop checks the release archive against the SHA-256 in the manifest. You can also install the native AI commands with scoop install blyx/linearfit blyx/residualwatch blyx/modelgate.

```
scoop bucket add blyx https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/scoop-blyx
scoop install blyx/blyx
blyxc --version
```

#### Install with Cargo

With Rust, Cargo and a host linker installed, build the compiler from crates.io. The version flag selects the same release as this course. Cargo normally places the result in the bin directory under your Cargo home.

```
cargo install --locked --version 0.2.1 blyxc
```

#### Check your installation

Open a fresh terminal after a PATH change. The version command should print blyxc 0.2.1. If the shell cannot find it, check the directory from which the executable runs directly and make sure that directory appears on PATH.

```
blyxc --version
```

#### Practice

Confirm which compiler your terminal will use if you have both a downloaded binary and a Cargo installation.

Hint

Use Get-Command blyxc in PowerShell or command -v blyxc in a POSIX shell.

Solution

The path should point to the installation you intended. Run that path with --version to verify it before continuing.

### [Create a project on disk](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/projects)

Move a program from the browser into a project, check the file and run it from a terminal.

#### Create a workspace

Choose a parent directory where you want to keep your work. This command creates a fresh directory named hello. Blyx refuses to create the project if that directory already exists, which helps protect existing work.

```
blyxc new hello
```

#### Find the entry point

The generated project contains Blyx.toml and src/main.blyx. The manifest records the project name, version and edition. The released CLI takes an explicit source file. Open hello/src/main.blyx in a text editor and find fn main().

#### Check, run and edit

From the same parent directory, run these commands in order. check parses the source. run executes it. The starter prints Hello, Blyx! Replace its print call with a calculation, save the file and run it again.

```
blyxc check hello/src/main.blyx
blyxc run hello/src/main.blyx
```

#### Keep paths consistent

If you change directory into hello, write src/main.blyx in subsequent commands. A file-not-found message is often a working-directory issue. The formatter rewrites the named file with normalized line endings.

```
blyxc fmt hello/src/main.blyx
```

#### Add a package to a native project

Clone a tagged Blyx library beside your entry file and import its public functions with use. The native runner and native build follow these local paths. The “Evaluate models with Blyx packages” chapter builds a working example. A Git submodule or a recorded commit keeps the dependency reproducible.

#### Practice

Make the starter print 21. Run a syntax check first and then execute the saved file.

Hint

In main, multiply 3 by 7 inside println!.

Solution

Use println!(3 * 7); and save. A successful check reports that the file parsed. The run command prints 21.

### [Develop in VS Code](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/editor)

Run an unsaved editor buffer, read a parser diagnostic and move the same program to the CLI.

#### Open a Blyx file

Install the desktop extension with ID RahulChaube.blyx-language. Open or create a file ending in .blyx. For an untitled buffer, select Blyx as its language. The editor highlighting helps you see strings, keywords and comments.

#### Run the active buffer

Use the play button in the editor title bar or choose Blyx: Run File in the Command Palette. The Blyx output channel shows the output for the current text, including unsaved edits. Paste the first tutorial program and change the string to confirm which version is running.

#### Read a diagnostic

Remove the closing brace of main and look in the Problems panel. A parser diagnostic reports where parsing ran into trouble. Restore the brace, wait for the parser to update and run again. Runtime failures, such as a zero integer divisor, appear when the program executes.

#### Use a local extension file

For an offline installation, download blyx-language-1.2.3.vsix from the editor release and choose Install from VSIX in the Extensions view. The extension uses a bundled WebAssembly interpreter. Save the source to disk before running a CLI command against that file.

#### Practice

Change a string without saving. Compare an editor run with a terminal run before and after saving.

Hint

The editor reads the buffer. The terminal reads the file on disk.

Solution

Before saving, the editor can print the new string while the CLI prints the old one. Save and run both again to compare the same source.

### [Debug and recover from errors](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/diagnostics)

Locate a syntax error, diagnose a runtime failure, and guard an operation using short-circuit evaluation.

#### Identify the failing stage

Check the file path first. A syntax error occurs while reading the program structure. A runtime error occurs while executing a valid expression with particular values. An error from a native build can point to a type mismatch or a missing Rust toolchain.

| Observation | Likely cause | First action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A parser line and column | Missing punctuation or an unfinished expression | Inspect that token and the preceding statement. |
| index … out of bounds | The index fell outside the vector | Check 0 <= i and i < len(v) before at. |
| dot requires vectors of equal length | The inputs contain different numbers of observations | Compare both lengths. |
| step limit exceeded | The budget ran out | Trace the loop condition and its updates. |

#### Reproduce the smallest failure

Save fn main() { println!(1 / 0); } as divide.blyx. A syntax check succeeds because the expression is well formed. Running it reports an integer division error and exits with code 4. Replace the zero with 2 and rerun. Whole-number division now prints 0.

#### Put a guard before division

The example reads count != 0 && total / count > 3. With a zero count the first comparison is false, so evaluation skips the division. Reversing the operands would evaluate the division before discovering the zero.

#### Limit a test run

A runaway loop can repeatedly evaluate valid code. Use a small positive budget while investigating it. The released interpreter also enforces a separate call-depth limit. Increasing the budget only helps after you have confirmed that the computation progresses.

```
blyxc run src/main.blyx --max-steps 10000
```

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn above_limit(total: i64, count: i64) -> bool {
    count != 0 && total / count > 3
}

fn main() {
    println!(above_limit(12, 0));
    println!(above_limit(12, 2));
}
```

Expected output

```
false
true
```

#### Practice

Make the second call use a nonzero count whose integer quotient is exactly three.

Hint

Keep total at 12 and choose a count that divides it evenly.

Solution

The quotient 12 / 4 is 3. The strict > 3 comparison returns false, and the zero-count case also returns false.

Find

```blyx
above_limit(12, 2)
```

Replace with

```blyx
above_limit(12, 4)
```

Output after the change

```
false
false
```

### [Build a native executable](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/native-builds)

Build an x86-64 program with Blyx Direct, reproduce the self-hosted compiler, or use the 0.2.1 toolchain for numerical workloads.

#### Build directly with Blyx Direct 0.1.0

Extract the Windows x64 or Linux x64 archive into its own directory. Its blyxc executable reads Blyx source and emits x86-64 instructions in a PE or ELF file. The build needs no external compiler, assembler or linker. This edition supports integer arithmetic, booleans, string literals, functions, recursion and loops. Save the short program below as double.blyx.

```
fn double(n: i64) -> i64 { n * 2 }
fn main() { println!(double(21)); }
```

[Download the self-hosted compiler](https://www.blyx-lang.space/download#direct)

#### Run the executable

On Linux, use the two commands below. In PowerShell use .\blyxc.exe build double.blyx -o double.exe followed by .\double.exe. The output should be 42. Choose a fresh filename for the executable.

```
./blyxc build double.blyx -o double
./double
```

#### Rebuild the compiler with itself

The archive includes compiler.blyx. On Linux the commands below compile it twice and compare the binaries. A successful comparison produces no output. The release test also runs generated applications with PATH empty. Preparing the very first seed from the Rust workspace is a separate build step.

```
./blyxc build compiler.blyx -o generation2
./generation2 build compiler.blyx -o generation3
cmp generation2 generation3
```

[Supported syntax and Windows verification commands](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyxxxx/tree/direct-v0.1.0/compiler/blyxc/bootstrap)

#### Start with a known result

Run the project source through the interpreter and keep a small expected output. When trying a native build for the first time, use the generated hello project or the capstone. Both have simple results that you can check by eye.

#### Build with the 0.2.1 toolchain

Use 0.2.1 for floating-point numbers, vectors, package imports and Apple Silicon macOS. Its build command translates the supported source to Rust and invokes rustc and a host linker. Use the command below with the 0.2.1 driver.

```
blyxc build src/main.blyx
```

#### Choose the output location

An explicit output name makes scripts easier to read. On Linux or macOS, run the executable using a relative path. Use a separate output path from the source file.

```
blyxc build src/main.blyx -o hello
./hello
```

#### Build on Windows

In PowerShell, use an .exe suffix and the current-directory prefix. The resulting executable runs independently of blyxc and rustc on a compatible machine.

```
blyxc build src/main.blyx -o hello.exe
.\hello.exe
```

#### Compare the two paths

Give numeric operands matching types and add explicit return types to functions that return values. The interpreter can promote mixed integer/float operations that a native build rejects. Check the executable's output using the same ordinary and boundary inputs you used for the interpreted run.

#### Build a program with imports

Native builds resolve local use paths and built-in host modules. The native runner builds the program and runs it in one step. Put program arguments after --. Use a normal build to keep an executable for repeated runs.

```
blyxc native-run src/main.blyx
```

#### Practice

Build the capstone source as a native executable, run it and compare the complete output with the chapter’s expected output.

Hint

Save the complete capstone program to src/main.blyx first.

Solution

The four readings sum to 123.5, two exceed 30, and the empty call prints no readings. Those three lines should agree across both execution paths.

## Language reference

### [Syntax, types and operators](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/language-reference)

Look up the executable forms, operator order and value types used in Blyx 0.2.1.

#### Read the shape of a program

A runnable source file declares top-level functions, including a parameterless main. A function body is a brace-delimited block of statements and an optional final expression. A semicolon ends a let declaration, return statement or expression statement. A final expression without one supplies the block’s value.

#### Read names, literals and comments

Choose a name such as sensor_count. Start with a letter or underscore and use letters, digits or underscores after it. Names are case-sensitive. The lexer reads 10, 0b1010, 0o12 and 0xA as the same integer. Use underscores to group long numbers and e for a decimal exponent. A line comment begins with //. A block comment begins with /* and ends with */. Block comments may nest.

#### Value types

Use explicit scalar types for native function parameters and results. Vector elements are numeric. A unit-valued block completes without returning a useful value.

| Type | Example | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| i64 | -12, 0, 42 | Checked integer arithmetic, counts and indices |
| f64 | 2.5, 1e-2 | Measurements, division with fractions and vector elements |
| bool | true, false | Conditions and logical combinations |
| str | "Blyx" | Text, labels and messages. The native subset also recognizes String. |
| vector | [2.0, 3.0] | An immutable sequence of numeric elements |
| unit (or omit the return annotation) | fn show() { println!(1); } | A function called for its effect |

#### Operator order

The rows are ordered from tightest binding to loosest among the operators used by the released interpreter here. Parentheses override the default order. Keep comparisons separate and join their boolean results with && or ||.

| Operators | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ! and unary - | Boolean negation and numeric negation | !ready, -x |
| * / % | Multiply, divide, remainder | 7 / 2 yields 3 |
| + - | Add, subtract | 2 + 3 * 4 yields 14 |
| < <= > >= | Order comparisons | t >= 30.0 |
| == != | Equality and inequality | count != 0 |
| && | Short-circuit logical AND | ready && valid |
| \|\| | Short-circuit logical OR | low \|\| high |
| = += -= *= /= %= | Assign to a mutable binding | count += 1 |

#### Declarations and control flow

let binds, let mut permits updates and fn introduces a function. if selects a branch, while checks before each pass, and loop repeats unconditionally. break leaves the nearest loop, continue begins its next iteration, and return exits the current function. Nested braces introduce a scope.

#### Literal and boundary behavior

The signed integer range is −9,223,372,036,854,775,808 through 9,223,372,036,854,775,807. Integer overflow and division by zero fail in the interpreter. f64 has finite precision and follows IEEE floating-point arithmetic. Many decimal fractions have only approximate binary representations. For native examples, use decimal literals consistently when a fractional result matters.

#### Text and escape sequences

Write strings in double quotes. Inside a string, \n starts a new line, \t inserts a tab, \" inserts a quote, and \\ inserts a backslash. Strings may contain Unicode text. Use several print! calls to combine text with values. The interpreter also reads a single-quoted character as one character of text. Use double-quoted text in code you plan to build natively.

#### Use a branch as a value

The classify function below uses if and else to produce a result. Both branch blocks end in string expressions and have the same result type. show returns unit and exists to print the result. The explicit -> unit annotation may be omitted there. Function parameters and any native return values use the types in the table above.

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn classify(n: i64) -> str {
    if n % 2 == 0 { "even" } else { "odd" }
}

fn show() -> unit {
    /* The three literals represent the same count. */
    println!(0b1010 == 0xA && 0o12 == 10);
    println!(1_000 + 5);
    println!(2.5e1);
    print!("label\t");
    println!(classify(10));
}

fn main() {
    show();
}
```

Expected output

```
true
1005
25
label	even
```

#### Practice

Change the classifier call to use the integer eleven in hexadecimal. Predict the final line and check whether the other lines change.

Hint

In hexadecimal, the digits after 9 are A, B, C, D, E and F. Eleven divided by two leaves a remainder of one.

Solution

0xB is eleven. classify chooses the odd branch, and the earlier calculations still use the original literals.

Find

```blyx
classify(10)
```

Replace with

```blyx
classify(0xB)
```

Output after the change

```
true
1005
25
label	odd
```

### [Built-in functions and output](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/builtin-reference)

Look up every vector built-in and both output macros, including their inputs, results and boundary cases.

#### Vector operations

All four functions receive vectors by value in Blyx source. The interpreter shares immutable element storage across calls. An index is an i64; an element, sum or dot product is an f64.

| Call | Result | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| len(vector) | i64 count, zero for an empty vector | len([4.0, 9.0]) → 2 |
| at(vector, i64) | The element at a zero-based index | at([4.0, 9.0], 1) → 9 |
| sum(vector) | Sum of the elements | sum([4.0, 9.0]) → 13 |
| dot(vector, vector) | Sum of products at matching indices | dot([1.0, 2.0], [4.0, 9.0]) → 22 |

#### Preconditions

at fails on a negative index, on index len(v), and on any access to an empty vector. dot fails if lengths differ, even when one side is empty. The sum of an empty vector and the dot product of two empty vectors are numerically zero. Check lengths before indexing or computing an average.

#### Output macros

print!() emits no text. println!() emits a newline. With a single expression, print!(value) displays its value, and println!(value) follows it with a newline. Use consecutive calls to combine text and numbers. Braces inside an output string are literal characters.

#### Cost of the operations

Reading the length or one element requires no scan. sum and dot visit the elements and their work grows with vector length. The interpreter charges its execution budget for these reductions. Holding the sum in a binding avoids recomputing it in every loop iteration.

#### Practice

Calculate dot([2.0, -1.0], [3.0, 4.0]) by hand. What happens if you remove the 4.0 from the second vector?

Hint

Multiply the corresponding entries before summing.

Solution

2 × 3 + (−1 × 4) is 2. After removing an entry the lengths differ, and the runtime reports an error.

### [Command-line reference](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/cli-reference)

Look up CLI forms, output files, execution budgets and exit codes.

#### Command forms

Pass the entry file to each command. Native builds and native-run also load its local imports. Quote any path containing spaces as required by your shell.

| Command | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| blyxc --version or -V | Print the installed compiler version. |
| blyxc help, --help or -h | Show the available commands. |
| blyxc new NAME | Create a new directory with Blyx.toml and src/main.blyx. |
| blyxc check FILE | Parse the file and report syntax diagnostics. |
| blyxc run FILE [--max-steps N] | Interpret main with an optional positive step budget. |
| blyxc build FILE [-o PATH] | Build a native executable, optionally at PATH. |
| blyxc native-run FILE [-- ARGS...] | Build the native project, run it and forward the program arguments. |
| blyxc fmt FILE | Rewrite the file with normalized line endings. |

#### Interpret the exit status

Capture the exit status immediately following the command. In PowerShell read $LASTEXITCODE. In a POSIX shell read $?. Scripts can use the status to decide whether to proceed. The exit codes below describe blyxc itself.

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Command completed successfully. |
| 1 | Examples include a missing file, parser error or failed build. |
| 2 | Examples include an unknown command, a missing argument or an invalid run budget. |
| 4 | The interpreter reached a runtime failure, such as integer division by zero. |

#### Find the output file

With no -o option a native build puts the executable beside the source, using the platform executable extension. Pass an explicit output name when a project has several programs or when a script needs to invoke a known path.

#### Separate execution budgets

--max-steps controls a CLI interpreter run. The browser and the VS Code worker also enforce source, output and time limits. A native executable has ordinary process and system limits. These modes can differ for a very long or deeply recursive computation.

#### Practice

Choose the commands for a script that first checks the syntax of main.blyx, then runs it with a budget of 500 steps.

Hint

Check the exit status before starting the second command.

Solution

Use blyxc check main.blyx, followed on success by blyxc run main.blyx --max-steps 500. A parser success does not guarantee that execution will finish within the budget.

### [What Blyx 0.2.1 can run](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/compatibility)

Choose an execution mode and identify features that are still being developed.

#### Choose an execution mode

Use the CLI interpreter or browser for immediate feedback. Use a native build to distribute a supported typed program to a compatible host. The editor and playground run the interpreter compiled to WebAssembly.

| Mode | Inputs and requirements | Limits to account for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Browser or desktop extension | A complete source buffer with fn main() | 256 KiB source, 64 KiB output and an eight-second worker deadline. |
| CLI interpreter | A .blyx file and the blyxc executable | Default one million evaluation steps and at most 64 simultaneous calls. |
| Native build | A supported typed program, rustc and a host linker | The generated program runs with system resources; interpreter step and call budgets do not apply. |

#### Supported execution

The teaching examples use functions, local bindings, scalar arithmetic, loops, recursion, numeric vectors and print macros. Native programs can import local .blyx modules and read command-line arguments or UTF-8 files through the host library. Use native-run or build for multi-file applications.

#### Features under development

The package registry and its dependency resolver are prototypes. The published source libraries use versioned Git checkouts. The browser and CLI interpreter execute a single source buffer. GPU kernels, a general tensor runtime, asynchronous tasks and actor scheduling remain development work.

#### Interpret a benchmark

Measure the same workload, input size and output across the implementations you compare. Separate startup costs from computational work when they answer different questions. The project’s published Fibonacci benchmark includes startup and reports its machine, raw samples and methodology.

#### Practice

Decide how to deliver a small numeric utility to a colleague who has no compiler installed. What do you need on each machine?

Hint

Distinguish the machine doing the build from the machine running the result.

Solution

On a suitable build host use blyxc, rustc and a linker to build the typed source. Deliver the executable for your colleague’s compatible OS and architecture. Try a small known input on the destination machine.
